concepts.name: Western Disturbances and Their Regional Impact
key_dimensions: Origin in Mediterranean Sea and extratropical cyclone mechanism vs. tropical cyclone confusion
Winter rainfall distribution: Punjab, Haryana, J&K vs. negligible impact on peninsular India
Role in Rabi crop cultivation and snowfall in Western Himalayas
Why Western Disturbances weaken progressively eastward across the Indo-Gangetic Plain

concepts.name: Monsoon Onset and Withdrawal Asymmetry Across Regions
key_dimensions: Southwest monsoon onset at Kerala (June 1) vs. withdrawal sequence starting from northwest Rajasthan (September)
Why onset is faster (40 days) but withdrawal is slower (nearly 3 months) — asymmetry trap
Northeast monsoon onset over Tamil Nadu (October-November) as a compensatory mechanism
Bay of Bengal branch vs. Arabian Sea branch: which reaches which region first and why

concepts.name: Rainfall Distribution: Windward vs. Leeward Effects (Orographic Rain Shadow)
key_dimensions: Western Ghats: heavy rainfall on Konkan/Malabar coast vs. rain shadow over Deccan Plateau (Pune, Nashik, Vidarbha)
Meghalaya highlands (Cherrapunji/Mawsynram) as world's highest rainfall vs. adjacent Shillong Plateau paradox
Himalayan southern slopes vs. Tibetan Plateau — orographic barrier role
UPSC trap: why Pune receives less rainfall than Mumbai despite being inland Maharashtra

concepts.name: Tamil Nadu's Unique Winter Rainfall Regime
key_dimensions: Why Tamil Nadu receives rainfall during October–December (retreating monsoon/NE monsoon) while rest of India dries
Tamil Nadu lies in rain shadow of SW monsoon — Arabian Sea branch blocked by Western Ghats
Bay of Bengal cyclones during retreating monsoon and their concentration on Coromandel Coast
Comparison with Kerala: both in peninsular south but opposite monsoon intensity patterns

concepts.name: Thar Desert Climate: Causes of Low Rainfall in Rajasthan
key_dimensions: Aravalli orientation parallel (not perpendicular) to Arabian Sea monsoon branch — no orographic lift trap
High temperature creating low pressure but moisture-deficient air — continental interior effect
Absence of Bay of Bengal branch penetration due to distance and terrain
Extreme diurnal temperature range and its contrast with coastal regions — continentality concept

concepts.name: Northeast India's High Rainfall Anomaly: Meghalaya and Assam
key_dimensions: Funnel effect of Bay of Bengal branch converging between Himalayas and Bangladesh hills
Cherrapunji vs. Mawsynram: which holds official record and why both are in Meghalaya (Khasi Hills orientation)
Brahmaputra valley flood regime linked to orographic rainfall patterns
Contrast with rain shadow areas immediately north (Assam plains vs. Meghalaya highlands)

concepts.name: Climate of the Coromandel Coast vs. Malabar Coast
key_dimensions: Coromandel: maximum rainfall in October–December (NE monsoon); Malabar: maximum in June–September (SW monsoon)
Both are eastern and western coastal strips yet completely opposite seasonal rainfall regimes
Cyclone vulnerability: Coromandel coast more prone than Malabar coast and the atmospheric reasons
Agricultural calendar differences arising from rainfall seasonality — UPSC applied angle

concepts.name: Himalayan Region Climate: Altitudinal Zonation and East-West Gradient
key_dimensions: Eastern Himalayas (Sikkim, Arunachal): high rainfall due to Bay of Bengal monsoon vs. Western Himalayas: drier, Western Disturbance-dependent
Altitudinal zones: Tropical→Subtropical→Temperate→Alpine→Tundra — temperature lapse rate application
Ladakh cold desert: lies in rain shadow of both Great Himalayas and Karakoram — double rain shadow trap
Snowmelt contribution to perennial rivers vs. rainfall-fed peninsular rivers — climate-hydrology linkage

concepts.name: Ladakh Cold Desert vs. Thar Hot Desert: Comparative Climate Analysis
key_dimensions: Both receive low rainfall (<200mm) but entirely different temperature regimes and causes
Ladakh: high altitude, double rain shadow, extreme cold; Thar: low altitude, continental, extreme heat
Vegetation and soil differences despite similar aridity — climate-biome relationship
UPSC trap: both called 'deserts' but mechanisms of aridity are fundamentally different

concepts.name: The Monsoon Trough and Its Northward Migration
key_dimensions: ITCZ-equivalent over India: monsoon trough position determines rainfall distribution in Indo-Gangetic Plain
Northward shift in July brings maximum rainfall to northern India; southward shift creates 'break monsoon'
Break monsoon conditions: dry spell in most of India but increased rainfall in northeast and Himalayan foothills
El Niño linkage: how ENSO displaces the monsoon trough — regional drought patterns

concepts.name: Regional Climatic Contrast: Mumbai vs. Chennai Annual Rainfall Comparison
key_dimensions: Mumbai (~2200mm, June–September) vs. Chennai (~1200mm, October–December) — same annual total illusion trap
Mumbai: orographic SW monsoon; Chennai: NE monsoon + occasional SW — dual source vs. single source
Flood vulnerability timing difference and urban planning implications
Why Mumbai has a distinct 4-month dry season while Chennai's dry season is June–September

concepts.name: Peninsular India's Climate Moderation by Seas: Thermal Contrast with Interior
key_dimensions: Peninsular tip (Thiruvananthapuram, Kanyakumari): equable climate due to sea influence on three sides
Deccan Plateau interior (Hyderabad, Nagpur): higher temperature range, semi-arid — continentality despite low latitude
Why low-latitude Nagpur is hotter in summer than high-latitude Delhi — altitude, distance from sea, and cloud cover factors
Marine influence decreasing gradient: coastal → interior plateau — isotherm pattern application

concepts.name: Assam and West Bengal Sub-Himalayan Belt (Duars/Terai) Rainfall Regime
key_dimensions: Among highest rainfall zones in India (>2500mm) due to Bay of Bengal branch impingement on Himalayan foothills
Terai belt as transition zone: high humidity, dense forests linked to orographic precipitation
Distinction between Ganga plains rainfall gradient (1200mm in west Bengal → 600mm in UP → 300mm in Rajasthan)
Why rainfall decreases westward along the IGP — progressive moisture loss from Bay of Bengal branch

concepts.name: Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and Its Differential Regional Impact on Indian Monsoon
key_dimensions: Positive IOD: warmer western Indian Ocean → enhanced moisture for Indian monsoon vs. negative IOD suppression
IOD vs. ENSO: independent and sometimes opposing effects — which dominates Indian regional rainfall
Regional differentiation: IOD more strongly affects peninsular India and Sri Lanka than northwest India
UPSC contemporary angle: 2019 positive IOD offsetting El Niño — good monsoon despite El Niño year

concepts.name: Cyclone-Prone Regions: Bay of Bengal vs. Arabian Sea Asymmetry
key_dimensions: Bay of Bengal generates ~5x more cyclones than Arabian Sea — warm SST, low salinity, weak vertical wind shear reasons
Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu coasts most vulnerable vs. Gujarat/Maharashtra occasionally affected
Post-monsoon (October–November) and pre-monsoon (April–May) as peak cyclone seasons — seasonal mechanism
Why Arabian Sea cyclones have intensified recently (climate change angle) — Oman, Gujarat recent events

concepts.name: Snowfall Regions and Their Climatic Drivers: J&K, Himachal, Uttarakhand
key_dimensions: Western Himalayas: snowfall primarily from Western Disturbances (winter) not monsoon
Eastern Himalayas (Sikkim, Arunachal): monsoon brings heavy snowfall at higher altitudes in summer
Snowline elevation differences: lower in western (drier air, less humid) vs. eastern Himalayas (wetter)
Impact of reduced Western Disturbances on Rabi crops and perennial river flow — hydrological consequence

concepts.name: The Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar Microclimate: Extreme Southern India
key_dimensions: Tamil Nadu's southernmost tip and Sri Lanka share similar NE monsoon rainfall regime — island proximity effect
Why Rameswaram and Pamban experience lower rainfall than rest of Tamil Nadu coast despite coastal location
Dry zone of southern Tamil Nadu (Tirunelveli, Thoothukudi) vs. wet zone (Nilgiris) within same state
Nilgiris: receives both SW and NE monsoon — one of few regions with bimodal rainfall peaks

concepts.name: Andaman & Nicobar vs. Lakshadweep: Island Climate Contrasts
key_dimensions: Andaman & Nicobar: first to receive SW monsoon (late May) — Bay of Bengal location, equatorial proximity
Lakshadweep: Arabian Sea, receives SW monsoon but lower intensity due to open ocean location
Both have equable maritime climate but Andaman has higher rainfall (3000mm+) vs. Lakshadweep (~1500mm)
UPSC trap: Andaman is NOT the southernmost point of India — Indira Point vs. common misconception

concepts.name: Climate of the Gangetic Plain: West-to-East Rainfall Gradient and Seasonal Temperature Extremes
key_dimensions: Rainfall decreases westward: Kolkata (~1600mm) → Patna (~1000mm) → Varanasi (~900mm) → Delhi (~600mm) → Amritsar (~500mm)
Western UP and Punjab: most extreme temperature range in India — continental interior, no sea moderation
'Loo' hot dry winds in summer (May–June) affecting Punjab to Bihar — regional wind specific to IGP
Winter fog in IGP: temperature inversion + moisture from soil + low wind speed — regional climate hazard with economic impact
